entries.topicDescription: Organizing code with Go modules and package conventions.

tips.title: Go modules manage dependencies with go.mod
tips.content:
Every Go project is a module, defined by a go.mod file at
the root. It declares the module path (which doubles as
the import path) and the Go version.

Use 'go mod init' to create a new module and 'go get' to
add dependencies. The go.sum file locks exact versions
with cryptographic checksums for reproducibility.

Go uses semantic versioning. Import paths include the
major version for v2+: "github.com/user/lib/v2". This
lets different major versions coexist in one project.

Run 'go mod tidy' regularly to remove unused dependencies
and add missing ones. It keeps your go.mod clean and your
builds reproducible.

tips.title: Package naming and structure conventions
tips.content:
Go packages are directories. The package name should be
short, lowercase, and singular: 'http' not 'httpUtils',
'user' not 'users'. Avoid stuttering: user.User is fine,
user.UserService is not.

Exported names start with uppercase, unexported with
lowercase. This is Go's access control — simple and
enforced by the compiler. No public/private keywords.

Organize by responsibility, not by type. Don't create
packages called 'models', 'utils', or 'helpers'. Instead,
group related functionality: 'auth', 'billing', 'email'.

The 'internal' directory is special: packages under it
can only be imported by code in the parent tree. Use it
for implementation details you don't want exposed.

tips.title: Init functions and blank imports for side effects
tips.content:
Each Go file can have an init() function that runs
automatically when the package is loaded — before main().
Multiple init functions per file and per package are allowed;
they run in declaration order.

Use init sparingly: for registering drivers, initializing
package-level variables, or validating configuration. Avoid
heavy work or anything that can fail silently.

Blank imports (_ "package") import a package solely for its
init side effects. The classic example is database drivers:
_ "github.com/lib/pq" registers the PostgreSQL driver with
database/sql.

Prefer explicit initialization (NewX functions) over init
when possible. Init functions make testing harder because
they run unconditionally.
